## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="g0-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Balance</dt><dd>Supply must equal demand at every moment. Prairie Town has no storage; real grids also use some, such as batteries (lesson 9).</dd>
<dt>Frequency</dt><dd>The alternating voltage completes 60 cycles each second, and generators turn in step with it; too little power slows them.</dd>
<dt>Variable and dispatchable plants</dt><dd>Wind and sun follow the weather; gas plants follow the operator's orders.</dd>
<dt>Ramp limit</dt><dd>The combined-cycle plant can change its output by only 40 MW from one hour to the next.</dd>
<dt>Merit order</dt><dd>Run the cheapest plant first and the most expensive last.</dd>
<dt>Decisions, goal, rules</dt><dd>What the operator chooses, what they keep low, and what they cannot break.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>The balance, energy and cost as equations</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

For every hour $t$, with $p_g(t)$ the output of plant $g$ in MW, $u(t)$ the [unserved]{.lx-term term="unserved-energy"} demand, $s(t)$ the [spilled]{.lx-term term="curtailment"} power and $d(t)$ the demand:

$$\sum_g p_g(t) + u(t) - s(t) = d(t).$$

Energy, cost and CO₂ are sums over the hours, with $\Delta t = 1$ hour, a running cost $c_g$ in \$/MWh and an operating emission rate $e_g$ in t/MWh (t = metric tonnes):

$$E_g = \sum_t p_g(t)\,\Delta t, \qquad C = \sum_t \sum_g c_g\,p_g(t)\,\Delta t, \qquad \mathrm{CO_2} = \sum_t \sum_g e_g\,p_g(t)\,\Delta t.$$

Check it on the cheapest-first rule's day:

- **Energy:** 2,400 MWh of nuclear, 1,960 MWh from the combined-cycle plant, 20 MWh from the peaker.
- **Cost:** $C = 2400 \times 10 + 1960 \times 40 + 20 \times 100 = \$104{,}400$.
- **CO₂:** $1960 \times 0.37 + 20 \times 0.55 = 736.2$ t, from the gas plants' fuel only.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Preview: the operator's day as an optimization problem</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Decisions</dt><dd>Each gas plant's output, every hour: 48 numbers.</dd>
<dt>Goal</dt><dd>The lowest gas running cost for the day. The flat nuclear output costs the same in every plan, so the goal leaves it out.</dd>
<dt>Rules</dt><dd>Supply equals demand each hour; each plant stays within its size; the combined-cycle changes by at most 40 MW an hour, starting from 115 MW at midnight.</dd>
</dl>
```

$$\min \; \sum_{t} \big( 40\,p_\mathrm{cc}(t) + 100\,p_\mathrm{pk}(t) \big)$$

| | Cheapest-first rule | Plan all 24 hours together |
|---|---|---|
| How it decides | one hour at a time | the whole day at once |
| Running cost | \$104,400 | \$104,000 |
| Peaker energy | 20 MWh | 0 MWh |

Planning saves \$400, about 0.4%, by warming the combined-cycle plant up before the solar dip and the sunset.

Every rule and the goal add up outputs times fixed numbers, so this is a [linear program]{.lx-term term="linear-program"}. [Lesson 10](10-write-it-down.qmd) writes it down step by step; [lesson 11](11-solver.qmd) hands it to a solver.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What the game leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Prairie Town is an island: it cannot buy power from its neighbours.</li>
<li>The forecast is perfect; real operators plan with forecasts that miss (lesson 4).</li>
<li>The game moves in one-hour steps; real grids balance second by second (lesson 3).</li>
<li>Nothing breaks: plants never fail, and power lines never fill up.</li>
<li>The frequency dial is an illustrative indicator: 0.01 Hz per MW out of balance, capped at 0.5 Hz either way. Real frequency depends on spinning machines and controls (lesson 3).</li>
<li>CO₂ counts only fuel burned at the plants. Building plants and supplying fuel, including methane leaks, are left out.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

::: {#check .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="g0-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="store" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A gas plant can save the electricity it makes and send it out later.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A gas plant makes electricity as it is used. Saving it for later takes <span class="lx-term" data-term="energy-storage">storage</span>, such as a battery or a pumped-storage hydro plant (lesson 9).</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="freq" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If supply is greater than demand, the grid's frequency rises.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. Extra power speeds up the spinning generators, so the <span class="lx-term" data-term="frequency">frequency</span> climbs above 60 Hz.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="wind" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A wind farm can be told to make more power when demand rises.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A wind farm can be turned down, but not up beyond what the wind allows: that is what <span class="lx-term" data-term="variable-renewables">variable</span> means.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="g0">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="gap" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">At 21:00 demand is 303 MW. Nuclear makes 100 MW, wind 98 MW, and the sun is down. How much must gas make?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">303 MW</li><li data-value="b">203 MW</li><li data-value="c">105 MW</li><li data-value="d">205 MW</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>105 MW: 303 − 100 − 98 = 105. Gas fills only the gap the other plants leave.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="energy" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">The peaker runs at 50 MW for 3 hours. How much <span class="lx-term" data-term="energy">energy</span> does it make?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">50 MWh</li><li data-value="b">150 MWh</li><li data-value="c">150 MW</li><li data-value="d">53 MWh</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>150 MWh: energy = power × time = 50 MW × 3 h. MW is a rate; an amount of energy is in MWh.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
:::

<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p><b>CO₂ per MWh.</b> Each hour's <span class="lx-term" data-term="carbon-intensity">CO₂ per MWh</span> depends on the mix. Under the cheapest-first rule, gas output peaks at 19:00, but CO₂ per MWh peaks at 00:00: gas is a bigger share of a smaller demand.</p>
<p><b>Real data.</b> U.S. grids report hourly demand and generation by fuel in EIA's <a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/">Hourly Electric Grid Monitor</a>.</p>
<p><b>Open code.</b> My <a href="https://github.com/Henryutd2021/ghg-load-regulation">open framework for carbon-aware electricity use</a> builds on those data.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Case file <a href="cf6-shifting-load-to-clean-hours.html">CF6</a> (average and marginal emission factors, and when moving electricity use to cleaner hours lowers CO₂).</p>
</div>
